Hosu.text: Hosu is a dense commuter city about 30 kilometers north of central Tokyo, half an hour out by express train, and it runs on the commuter clock. Elevated rail lines cross it in every direction on concrete overpasses. Platforms are packed at dawn and dusk, downtown goes quiet at midday, and izakaya and karaoke bars keep the side streets busy until the last train; after that the back lanes go dark and empty. Hosu Downtown is a grid of office towers, banks, a department store and chain restaurants along Main Street, which runs north from Hosu Station, with a police box and a giant news screen on the Station Plaza. Southwest of the station, the older quarter of the Hosu Back Alleys packs four- to six-story blocks wall to wall, with lanes too narrow for cars and rooftops crowded with water tanks and air-conditioning units, where residents dry laundry by day. Most people here are office workers, shopkeepers and families in aging apartment blocks. Hosu has few heroes for its size. The big agencies sit in central Tokyo, and a call from downtown can wait ten minutes or more for a pro, which shop owners complain about openly. Small local agencies share the patrols with the city police under Chief Kenji Tsuragamae: Manual runs a careful, by-the-book agency near the station, and Native walks Main Street on foot. Hosu General Hospital handles the city's emergencies, and patrol heroes with movement Quirks treat the rooftops as their fastest routes across town.
